claims.text: High-temperature plastic strain and toughness in fusion plasma-facing tungsten alloys are predominantly governed by the balance between thermally activated dislocation climb and constrained grain-boundary sliding.
A uniform nanoscale dispersion of oxide nanoparticles mediates the balance between dislocation climb and grain-boundary sliding.
Oxide nanoparticles pin grain boundaries and dislocations in tungsten.
At high temperature, oxide-mediated pinning promotes dynamic recovery while preventing abrupt crack initiation.
Internal oxidation or mechanical alloying followed by consolidation can introduce a well-dispersed, modest volume fraction of stable oxide nanoparticles into tungsten.
The relevant oxide dispersion consists of nanoscale particles distributed along grain boundaries and within grains.
Oxide particles impede excessive grain-boundary sliding.
Oxide particles impede dislocation pileup.
Impeded grain-boundary sliding and dislocation pileup promote thermally activated dislocation climb and dynamic recovery.
Dislocation climb and dynamic recovery provide controlled accommodation of plastic strain.
Controlled accommodation of plastic strain delays strain localization and crack initiation.
Delaying strain localization and crack initiation enhances high-temperature toughness.
Compared with tungsten having minimal oxide dispersion, oxide-dispersed tungsten will exhibit greater plastic strain before failure.
Compared with tungsten having minimal oxide dispersion, oxide-dispersed tungsten will exhibit increased fracture toughness.
Compared with tungsten having minimal oxide dispersion, oxide-dispersed tungsten will absorb more energy during high-temperature deformation.
Oxide-dispersed tungsten will show more homogeneous dislocation activity and reduced grain-boundary stress concentration than the undoped baseline.
The hypothesis is expected to hold for tungsten and tungsten-based alloys above 1000°C when the oxide volume fraction is moderate.
The hypothesis may not apply to FCC or complex intermetallic systems with different deformation mechanisms.
Excessive oxide content can cause embrittlement and place the material outside the proposed beneficial regime.
Oxide type, particle size, and volume fraction have an unresolved optimum for maximizing toughness without embrittlement, and radiation-defect interactions are not captured.
